This is a pattern we see repeated in history, explaining why myths are constructed in certain ways. Another metaphor to consider is that myths and stories are like house renovations. When you renovate a house, you add different layers; similarly, myths build upon earlier narratives. We'll look at one final story to illustrate this process.

Remember they used writing to gaslight the people. Even though Samaria Mesopotain was developing rapidly, as seen on this map, it remained diverse with different forms of industry and economy. For example, in green areas, agriculture thrives, while red areas focus on pastoral activities like raising sheep and goats.

King or priest: Which type do you prefer?

Agriculture. Obviously, agriculture. Why? Because it's easier to control.

They will create mythologies to convince people to give up the free lifestyle of a pastoralist and become enslaved farmers. This is known as the debate between the sheep and the grain. The sheep argues that it is better than the grain, providing clothing, sandals, oil, and food for soldiers. In contrast, the grain claims superiority through its role in sacrifices and preparation of beer.

The argument from the sheep goes like this: "I provide white wool clothes, making the king joyful on his throne. I walk with priests to holy meals." The grain retorts: "When beer is prepared, my produce stands separate from yours. My farmer chases away your herdsmen."
